chapter_title: Smart Pointers and Resource Management with STL

screens.title: Smart Pointers and Resource Management with STL
screens.subtitle: RAII, unique_ptr, shared_ptr, weak_ptr, and make_* helpers

narration.text: In this lesson we'll tie together RAII and the smart pointers in the standard library so you can manage dynamic resources with confidence. You will see how ownership models—exclusive, shared, and observing—map to std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr, and std::weak_ptr, and why prefering make_unique and make_shared improves safety and performance. We will ground each idea with short code examples and a small hands-on Document manager exercise so you leave with patterns you can apply right away. Expect to learn which pointer to choose when a single owner must exist, when many parts share a resource, and how to avoid cycles that leak memory. I will also call out common mistakes like mixing raw pointers with smart pointers and when to supply a custom deleter. By the end you'll be able to pick the right smart pointer for a scenario, recognize ownership relationships in your design, and apply RAII idioms to reduce leaks and dangling pointers. Think about a real object in your codebase: who should own it, who should share access, and who should only observe it?

keyIdea.title: Chapter focus
keyIdea.text: Use RAII and smart pointers to make dynamic resource management safe and explicit: unique_ptr for single ownership, shared_ptr for shared ownership, weak_ptr to observe without owning.

narration.text: This chapter revisits RAII and makes ownership explicit through smart pointers. By the end you will be able to explain RAII as tying resource lifetime to object lifetime and why that prevents leaks. You will implement exclusive ownership with std::unique_ptr, transferring ownership with move semantics, and use std::make_unique to allocate safely. You will also use std::shared_ptr to share resources across multiple owners, inspect use_count for diagnostics, and prefer std::make_shared for efficiency. Finally, you will use std::weak_ptr as a non-owning observer to break cyclic references that would otherwise cause leaks. Each objective includes a small practice or code pattern: create a unique_ptr and move it, copy a shared_ptr into several holders and observe use_count, and replace a back-reference with weak_ptr to see destruction happen. Achieving these objectives will make your dynamic memory management safer and clearer. As you learn, ask yourself for each object: who must own it, who must share it, and who needs only to observe it?

screens.title: RAII — the foundation for smart pointers
screens.subtitle: Tie resource ownership to object lifetime

narration.text: RAII stands for Resource Acquisition Is Initialization. It means you should acquire a resource in a constructor and release it in a destructor so the resource's lifetime matches the object's lifetime. This idiom is fundamental because it makes resource management deterministic: when the object leaves scope, the destructor runs and cleans up. A concrete example is wrapping a file handle in a class whose destructor closes the file. In this chapter, smart pointers implement RAII for heap-allocated objects: the smart pointer's destructor deletes the underlying object if it owns one. A common misconception is thinking RAII is only about memory; RAII applies to any resource—memory, sockets, file descriptors, locks—anything that needs deterministic cleanup. Another misconception is believing smart pointers remove the need to think about ownership; they make ownership explicit, so you must still decide which parts of code own or share a resource. Example: if a logger object is created inside a scope and owned by a unique_ptr, it will be destroyed when the unique_ptr leaves scope; if instead you place shared_ptr copies into subscribers, the logger will live until the last shared_ptr is gone. Key takeaway: RAII gives deterministic cleanup and smart pointers are the idiomatic RAII wrapper for heap objects. Ask yourself: which object should be responsible for releasing this resource?

keyIdea.title: RAII principle
keyIdea.text: Acquire in constructor, release in destructor. Smart pointers implement RAII for dynamically allocated objects.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › RAII — Definition
Definition and claim

RAII ties resource lifetime to object lifetime so resources are released deterministically in destructors.

Why it matters
  • Deterministic cleanup reduces leaks and makes code easier to reason about.
  • Works naturally with scope and exceptions: destructors always run on scope exit.
  • Smart pointers bring RAII to heap objects so you avoid manual delete calls.
Key Takeaway

Always bind ownership to an object's lifetime. Smart pointers are the RAII containers for heap allocations.

Concrete example
Imagine a file wrapper that opens in the constructor and closes in the destructor. Replace the raw file pointer with a smart pointer for heap objects and the destructor will call delete automatically when the smart pointer goes out of scope.
Common misconception

Smart pointers eliminate the need to think about ownership. They help, but you must still choose the correct ownership model: unique ownership vs shared ownership vs observation.

Check your understanding

Name a resource in your code that benefits from RAII and explain which object should own it and why.

narration.text: std::unique_ptr enforces exclusive ownership. Only one unique_ptr can own a particular object at a time; ownership is transferable through move semantics. This makes unique_ptr ideal when one component must be the sole manager of a resource, for example a manager that creates and destroys a Robot when the manager is destroyed. unique_ptr is almost as cheap as a raw pointer because it stores only the pointer and an optional custom deleter. The preferred creation method is std::make_unique which performs allocation and construction in a single step and is exception-safe. A concrete example from the chapter shows creating a MyResource via make_unique, calling its operation, and then moving the unique_ptr into a function which takes ownership. A common mistake is attempting to copy a unique_ptr; such code fails at compile time. Another pitfall is extracting the raw pointer with get() and passing it to code that might delete it; that can cause double delete. Key takeaway: prefer unique_ptr for single-ownership cases and use move semantics to transfer ownership clearly. A quick design check: if there should never be more than one owner, use unique_ptr.

keyIdea.title: unique_ptr summary
keyIdea.text: Exclusive ownership, move-only, prefer std::make_unique, avoid copying and unsafe raw pointer transfers.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › std::unique_ptr
Core behavior

unique_ptr models exclusive ownership. It is move-only which prevents accidental sharing and double deletes when used correctly.

Best practice
  • Prefer std::make_unique for creation.
  • Transfer ownership with std::move explicitly.
  • Store unique_ptrs in containers by moving them.
Concrete example
#include <memory>
// Preferred creation
std::unique_ptr<MyResource> r = std::make_unique<MyResource>(1);
// Transfer ownership
std::unique_ptr<MyResource> r2 = std::move(r);
// r is now empty; r2 owns the resource
Common mistakes
  • Trying to copy a unique_ptr (compile-time error).
  • Calling get() and letting external code delete the raw pointer—double delete risk.
  • Using shared_ptr where unique_ptr would suffice and add unnecessary overhead.
Key Takeaway

Use unique_ptr for single-owner semantics and move ownership explicitly. Use make_unique for safety.

screens.title: Moving unique_ptr — ownership transfer
screens.subtitle: How and when to move ownership safely

narration.text: Moving a unique_ptr transfers ownership from one owner to another. The source unique_ptr becomes empty and the destination becomes the sole owner. This move is explicit and cheap: it typically copies the raw pointer and sets the source to null. A common scenario is creating a unique_ptr in a factory or function and returning it to the caller; move semantics make this safe. For example, construct a MyResource with make_unique and then call another function that takes a unique_ptr by value. That function becomes the new owner and will destroy the resource when it goes out of scope. When placing unique_ptrs in containers, push_back must receive a moved unique_ptr; you cannot copy into the container. A misconception is that moving a unique_ptr invalidates the pointed object; it does not — only ownership changes. Another pitfall is attempting to use the source after moving without checking for null. Key practice: after moving, check the source pointer or structure your code so the source isn’t used afterwards. This ensures the resource is owned by exactly one manager and cleaned up deterministically. Moving unique_ptr — ownership transfer means std::move hands over ownership. the moved-from unique_ptr becomes empty; the moved-to unique_ptr owns the object.. In practical terms, how and when to move ownership safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Move semantics
keyIdea.text: std::move hands over ownership. The moved-from unique_ptr becomes empty; the moved-to unique_ptr owns the object.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Moving unique_ptr
Step-by-step ownership transfer
1. Create with make_unique
std::unique_ptr<T> p = std::make_unique<T>(args);
2. Move to another owner
std::unique_ptr<T> q = std::move(p); // p becomes empty
3. Pass into functions
void process(std::unique_ptr<T> in) { /* owns it */ }
Concrete code snippet
#include <memory>
void process(std::unique_ptr<MyResource> r) {
  if (r) r->operation();
} 

std::unique_ptr<MyResource> a = std::make_unique<MyResource>(1);
process(std::move(a)); // ownership moved; 'a' is now empty
Common pitfall

Do not use the moved-from pointer without checking; it may be null and using it causes runtime errors.

screens.title: std::shared_ptr — Shared ownership and reference counting
screens.subtitle: When multiple owners need access

narration.text: std::shared_ptr implements shared ownership using reference counting. Multiple shared_ptr instances can point to the same object; the resource is destroyed automatically when the last shared_ptr is destroyed or reset. This model fits scenarios where ownership is distributed across subsystems, for instance a shared Document used by a UI and a background worker. The chapter example constructs a MyResource with make_shared, copies it into several shared_ptrs, and prints use_count to demonstrate the count increasing and decreasing as copies are created and go out of scope. A common misconception is thinking shared_ptr removes the need to reason about lifetime; it delays destruction until the last owner is gone, so cycles created by mutual shared_ptrs prevent destruction entirely. Another trade-off is a small runtime cost and an additional control block allocation unless make_shared is used, which typically performs one allocation for object and control block. Key takeaway: use shared_ptr when true sharing is required, but prefer unique_ptr when possible. Ask: do multiple independent owners logically need to share ownership of this object? std::shared_ptr — Shared ownership and reference counting means shared ownership via reference counting; prefer make_shared to reduce allocations; watch for cycles.. In practical terms, when multiple owners need access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: shared_ptr summary
keyIdea.text: Shared ownership via reference counting; prefer make_shared to reduce allocations; watch for cycles.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › std::shared_ptr
How reference counting works

Each shared_ptr points to a control block that tracks how many shared_ptrs and weak_ptrs reference the object. When the last shared_ptr is destroyed, the object is deleted.

When to use
  • When multiple independent owners need a shared resource.
  • When lifetime cannot be determined by a single scope.
Concrete example
// Create and copy
std::shared_ptr<MyResource> a = std::make_shared<MyResource>(10);
std::shared_ptr<MyResource> b = a; // use_count increases
{
  std::shared_ptr<MyResource> c = a; // use_count increases again
}
// use_count decreases when c is destroyed
Trade-offs & pitfalls
  • Overhead from reference counting and control block allocations.
  • Risk of cyclic references if bidirectional shared_ptrs are used.
  • Prefer make_shared to allocate control block and object together.
Key Takeaway

Use shared_ptr when true shared ownership is needed, but remain mindful of cycles and allocation costs.

narration.text: std::make_unique and std::make_shared are the preferred ways to construct smart pointers. make_unique performs allocation and constructs the object, returning a unique_ptr; make_shared constructs the object and the control block in one allocation in most implementations. This single-allocation behavior makes make_shared more efficient than constructing a shared_ptr with new because it often avoids a separate control block allocation. Both helpers improve exception safety by ensuring no leak occurs if construction throws. A concrete example: using std::make_shared<MyResource>(10) creates a shared_ptr whose use_count starts at one; copying that shared_ptr increases the count without extra allocations. A common misunderstanding is thinking make_shared is always superior; choose make_unique for unique ownership. Also avoid make_shared for very large objects if memory layout requirements or custom deleters make separate allocations preferable. Key takeaway: prefer make_unique for exclusive ownership and make_shared for shared ownership when standard control-block semantics are acceptable and you want improved allocation efficiency. make_unique vs make_shared means make_unique and make_shared offer exception safety and efficiency; pick the helper that matches ownership semantics.. In practical terms, why factory helpers matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Factory helpers
keyIdea.text: make_unique and make_shared offer exception safety and efficiency; pick the helper that matches ownership semantics.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › make_unique vs make_shared
make_unique

Used to create std::unique_ptr safely and efficiently. It prevents leaks if construction throws.

auto u = std::make_unique<Document>("Title","Content");
Best when ownership is exclusive.
make_shared

Creates std::shared_ptr and its control block efficiently, often in a single allocation.

auto s = std::make_shared<Document>("Meeting","Notes");
std::cout << s.use_count() << std::endl; // typically 1
Best when objects are shared across multiple owners.
Key Takeaway

Use factory helpers to get exception-safe allocation and construction. Choose make_unique for unique ownership and make_shared when you need shared ownership and allocation efficiency.

screens.title: std::weak_ptr — Observing without owning
screens.subtitle: Break cycles and check liveness safely

narration.text: std::weak_ptr is a non-owning smart pointer used to observe objects managed by shared_ptr without increasing the reference count. It is essential for breaking cyclic dependencies that would otherwise keep objects alive forever. A typical pattern is a parent with shared_ptr to child and child holding a weak_ptr back to the parent. The weak_ptr does not prevent destruction; to access the object safely you call lock() which returns a shared_ptr if the object still exists or an empty shared_ptr if it has been destroyed. A concrete example from the chapter shows classes A and B where A owns B via shared_ptr and B observes A via weak_ptr. When local shared_ptrs go out of scope, weak_ptrs do not stop destruction and lock() returns empty. A common misconception is trying to dereference weak_ptr directly; it offers no operator* or operator-> because it does not guarantee liveness. Another pitfall is confusing weak_ptr with a mere raw observer: weak_ptr provides a safe way to check and acquire temporary ownership. Key takeaway: use weak_ptr for back-references and observers, and always check lock() before use. std::weak_ptr — Observing without owning means non-owning observer to break cycles; use lock() to obtain a temporary shared_ptr if the object still exists.. In practical terms, break cycles and check liveness safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: weak_ptr role
keyIdea.text: Non-owning observer to break cycles; use lock() to obtain a temporary shared_ptr if the object still exists.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › std::weak_ptr
Why weak_ptr exists

To observe objects managed by shared_ptr without contributing to their lifetime, so cycles can be broken and memory freed.

Example pattern
// A owns B, B observes A
std::shared_ptr<A> a = std::make_shared<A>();
std::shared_ptr<B> b = std::make_shared<B>();
a->b_ptr = b; // shared ownership of B
b->a_ptr = a; // weak_ptr does NOT increase A's use_count
Using lock()

Call lock() to attempt to obtain a shared_ptr. If lock() returns empty, the observed object was destroyed.

Common mistake

Don't assume weak_ptr points to a live object. Always test the result of lock() before using the resource.

Key Takeaway

Use weak_ptr to break cycles and safely observe objects; acquire temporary ownership with lock() when needed.

narration.text: Let's walk through the Document manager starter code focusing on unique_ptr usage. The Document class prints messages on construction and destruction so you can observe lifetime. In main, create a unique_ptr using std::make_unique. Call print to verify access. Then move the unique_ptr to another unique_ptr variable to simulate handing the document to a different manager. The original pointer becomes empty and should not be used further; checks for null are recommended after a move. This pattern demonstrates exclusive ownership: only one manager owns the document at any time and when that manager goes out of scope the Document destructor runs. A common misconception is thinking moving a unique_ptr copies the object; it only transfers ownership of the pointer. Another practical note is storing unique_ptrs in containers: you must move them into the container, not copy. Key takeaway: use unique_ptr for objects with a single logical owner and instrument your code with simple print statements in constructors and destructors to validate lifetime behavior during testing. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Document Manager — unique_ptr
Starter code snippet
#include <memory>
#include <iostream>

std::unique_ptr<Document> doc1 = std::make_unique<Document>("Report Q1","Sales figures are up.");
doc1->print();

std::unique_ptr<Document> doc2 = std::move(doc1); // ownership moved
if (!doc1) std::cout << "doc1 is now empty." << std::endl;
Run this to see constructor and destructor messages. The destructor runs when doc2 leaves scope, confirming unique ownership.
Checklist
  • Create with make_unique.
  • Transfer with std::move explicitly.
  • After move, do not dereference the source without checking for null.
Key Takeaway

unique_ptr models exclusive ownership. Use moves to transfer ownership and validate lifetime by observing constructor/destructor output during testing.

narration.text: Now consider shared access: use std::shared_ptr when several parts of your program need to hold a reference. In the Document manager exercise, create a shared_ptr with std::make_shared and push copies into a vector to simulate multiple users. Each copy increases the reference count. You can print use_count at various points to observe the number of owners. When you reset one shared_ptr or a scope ends, the count decreases; when the count reaches zero, the Document is destroyed. A common misconception is relying solely on use_count for correctness; use_count helps debugging but doesn't replace sound ownership design. Another pitfall is putting shared_ptrs into structures that outlive the resource's logical lifetime, inadvertently keeping it alive. Key practice: prefer shared_ptr only when multiple independent owners are required, and remove references deliberately to allow destruction. Example: create a shared Document, push it into a vector, print use_count before and after resetting the original shared_ptr to observe the expected change. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: shared_ptr in practice
keyIdea.text: Use shared_ptr for multiple owners, monitor use_count to understand lifetimes, and ensure references are released when no longer needed.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Document Manager — shared_ptr
Sample code
#include <memory>
#include <vector>

auto sdoc = std::make_shared<Document>("Meeting Notes","..." );
std::cout << sdoc.use_count() << std::endl; // 1
std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Document>> v;
v.push_back(sdoc); // count 2
v.push_back(sdoc); // count 3
std::cout << sdoc.use_count() << std::endl; // 3
sdoc.reset(); // original reset, vector still holds copies
std::cout << v[0].use_count() << std::endl; // 2
Observe when the Document is destroyed: after the last shared_ptr in the vector is destroyed or cleared.
Design questions
  • Who logically needs to keep the object alive?
  • Can ownership be narrowed to a single manager instead?
  • Are there potential cycles among owners?
Common pitfall

Leaving shared_ptrs in long-lived containers can unintentionally extend object lifetime. Manage container lifetimes deliberately.

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety notes
screens.subtitle: Mixing raw pointers, cycles, and custom deleters

narration.text: This screen collects the common mistakes you must avoid. First, mixing raw pointers and smart pointers can lead to double deletion or use-after-free if raw pointers are deleted elsewhere. Avoid passing raw pointers from smart_ptr. get() to code that might assume ownership. Second, cyclic shared_ptr references cause leaks because reference counts never reach zero. Replace back-references with weak_ptr to allow cleanup. Third, creating smart pointers with new instead of make_* loses exception safety and can produce extra allocations; prefer factory helpers. Fourth, when resources are not freed by delete—like FILE handles or OS descriptors—provide custom deleters to smart pointers so RAII still applies. A misconception is that shared_ptr always cleans up cycles; it does not. Another is believing use_count is a full correctness test—use_count is a debugging aid but not a synchronization tool in multithreaded contexts. Key takeaway: pick the right pointer for the job, avoid unsafe raw-pointer transfers, and use weak_ptr or custom deleters where required to maintain safe RAII. Common mistakes and safety notes means don't mix ownership models unsafely, avoid shared_ptr cycles, use make_* helpers, and supply custom deleters for non-delete cleanup.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Don't mix ownership models unsafely, avoid shared_ptr cycles, use make_* helpers, and supply custom deleters for non-delete cleanup.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Common Mistakes & Safety
Mixing raw & smart pointers

Do not transfer ownership by giving out raw pointers returned from get() to code that may delete them. Smart pointers should remain the sole owners unless ownership is explicitly transferred.

Custom deleters
For resources not freed by delete, pass a custom deleter to the smart pointer so RAII still performs correct cleanup.
Cyclic dependencies

If two objects hold shared_ptrs to each other, their reference counts never reach zero. Use weak_ptr for the back-reference to break the cycle and allow destruction.

Debug tip

Use simple constructor/destructor print messages while testing to confirm objects are destroyed when you expect.

Key Takeaway

Follow ownership rules strictly, use weak_ptr to break cycles, and prefer make_* helpers. When in doubt, choose the least-permissive ownership model that meets requirements.
